newsitem.title: RUSSIA: OPINION - Russian economy on track - Jochen Wermut.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Russian economy on track - Jochen Wermut.

text.p: By Jochen Wermuth, head of the Economic Expert Group, Ministry of Finance, Russian Federation

MOSCOW, Nov 22 - As with "the end of reforms" after Mr Gaidar's dismissal in late 1992, the "end of stabilisation" after Mr Fyodorov quit as Finance Minister in late 1993, the dismissal of Mr Chubais in early 1996 and the supposed "end of reforms", the supposed "financial crisis" in the fall of 1996 never happened.
In fact, five weeks before the end of the year, Russian finances are soundly on track in spite of the costs of political uncertainty throughout 1996.
WHY DOOMSDAY FORECASTS HAVE MISSED THE POINT
This is thanks to the fact that the Government and Monetary Authorities have held a firm course on economic policy for 1996 as a whole, and in particular for the second half of 1996.

In fact both money supply growth and the primary deficit are well below initial targets. Even in the run-up to the presidential elections, the Government tightened non-interest expenditure relative to revenue (the primary deficit) both compared to the primary deficit in 1995 and the primary deficit initially envisaged.

This occurred in spite of declining revenues in order to compensate for increased domestic interest expenditure. The latter were due to political uncertainty and the conservative approach to opening up domestic markets to short-term portfolio investors given the Mexican experience.
EVEN MORE PRUDENCE AFTER PRESIDENTIAL ELECTIONS
Only three days after election day the Government decided to set out on an even firmer policy course for second half 1996.

To reduce interest rates on domestic debt, the Government decided to cut the primary deficit by about two percentage points of GDP more than initially envisaged for the second half of 1996, and to reduce net financing on the T-bill market. Indeed, both in September and the first 20 days of November the Government was running a primary surplus, putting it well on track for its overall deficit target for the year as a whole.

The other main problems the Government started to tackle more agressively after the elections were cash revenue collection and enforcement of bankruptcies. Both had been neglected to some extent in the run-up to the elections. As a first step, the Government imposed a package of over 30 measures, abolishing means of non-cash tax payments and closing loopholes in the tax system.
With these measures in place by late August, enterprises were put in a difficult position of having to actually put up cash and account for all their debts.
As a result in September, tax revenue fell to record lows for the year as a whole. Initial estimates put revenue as low as 11 trillion roubles, alerting many observers.
REVENUES ARE RECOVERING

Final figures however put cash revenues already at close to 13 trillion roubles. In October, cash revenue collection to the federal budget reached almost 17 trillion roubles, and for the first 20 days of November, the Government collected revenue at a monthly rate of 25 trillion roubles. At about 12 percent of GDP this is well above the historic level of federal budget revenue.
Final official figures for November will only be available by mid-December, but the trend is already more than clear today.

So why is there no "hot autumn" in spite of "huge wage arrears"? Because firstly wage arrears of the federal budget are relatively limited at about 1 trillion roubles, and secondly, in real terms, budget revenue and budget expenditure are not significantly lower than in 1995.
The main problem in 1996 was that inflation, GDP and budget revenues were severely overstated in the budget as the very unfortunate result of a political bargaining process.

The Government is thus not able to meet its expenditure target in full and is keeping expenditure to the sum of revenue actually collected and its deficit target -- a policy already followed in 1992, 1993 and 1994.
Finally, consumption has already fallen between 1995 and 1996, which unfortunately means that most of the fall in GDP in 1996 is due to a fall in investments.
CHIEF TASK IS BOOSTING PRIVATE INVESTMENT
In this situation it remains the main aim of Government policy to reduce its deficit and domestic interest rates in order to stimulate private sector investment again.
An important part of this policy is to diversify sources of non-inflationary deficit financing by tapping international capital markets.
This effort has been backed by the fact that in addition to traditional surveys of Russia's policies, three credit rating agencies evaluated Russia's medium-term outlook very positively.

This assessment was better than the dim picture still drawn by the western press, and the perception of market participants. Looking at the breathtaking progress made over the past four years, it cannot be denied that in the Russian Federation the foundations for sustainable growth have been laid.

Of course it is theoretically possible to spoil any party, but this one is getting harder and harder to spoil, in particular if the right decisions continue to be taken and the lessons of 1996 are learnt.
